text.p: In mid-May 1947 I was drafting a list a questions to ask Mohammad Ali Jinnah, who would soon become the founder of the new nation of Pakistan.

After drafting several questions, I asked office colleagues of the Associated Press of India (API), the Indian domestic news agency, then owned by Reuters: "If Jinnah offered to answer for publication, what would be the most newsworthy question you could ask him today?"
K.S. Ramachandran, the most senior and able of them all, shot back: "Ask him if he will demand a corridor."

Pakistan, to be carved out of the Indian sub-continent in August 1947, was to comprise two portions -- West Pakistan, to the west of India, and East Pakistan, to India's east. A corridor of land running through India could have connected the two.
East Pakistan broke away in 1971 and became modern-day Bangladesh.
GOOD QUESTION

I rated Ramachandran as the best news-getter in Delhi -- a small, wiry, touchy character who seemed to have near instant access to Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Mohammad Ali Jinnah and every other Indian who mattered.

As president of the All India Muslim League, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, also known as Quaid-i-Azam or "great leader", was a power in the land who had already received a personal note from Lord Louis Mountbatten, then Viceroy of India.
Ramachandran's question seemed thoroughly relevant so it went in as question seven or eight: "Will you demand a corridor through Hindustan connecting eastern and western Pakistan states?"
Days later Jinnah's secretary telephoned to say the Quaid-i-Azam had answered all my questions. I shot round to Jinnah's residence, to find a typewritten text of answers.
Against the corridor question, Jinnah had answered "Yes".
"Will he enlarge on that?" I asked. "Maybe indicate what length and breadth of corridor he has in mind, what route it might take and so on?" The secretary said he would not.
I ran the story straight -- question and answer in the usual way.
ALL HELL BREAKS LOOSE

The API however led with the corridor -- Mohammed Ali Jinnah today demanded a corridor linking East and West Pakistan -- and all hell broke loose. Almost every paper in India seemed to go to town on the story.
One national editorialised: "Who is this sinister agent of Reuters in our midst...Is this the prelude to a trade pact between Reuters and Pakistan?"
I telephoned John Turner, head of Reuters in India based in Bombay: "Want me to beat it quick?" I asked. "Why?" said John.
"I think it's pretty obvious from the treatment of the Jinnah interview," I said. "Who in government is going to talk to me here now?"
"Forget it," John retorted. "A rattling good story -- just look at the way the papers have gobbled it up."
Jawaharlal Nehru, soon to be independent India's first prime minister, was quoted as saying: "The demand for a corridor is fantastic and absurd."

The interview gave the press attache to the Viceroy an entry for his Viceroy's House Diary: "Jinnah has dropped a carefully timed and placed bombshell. He demands a 300 mile corridor to link West and East Pakistan. The technique of realising it seems to have been copied from Stalin.

"Doon Campbell of Reuters to whom the story was given told me it was in answer to a questionnaire which he had lodged with Jinnah some days previously. No one was more surprised than he to find himself with such a scoop on his hands."
SUITABLY REPRIMANDED
A wise and typically Indian formula got me off the hook in the immediate emotional aftermath of my "corridor" interview.
In the highly charged atmosphere of communal suspicion which pervaded Delhi, I could expect an accusatory finger pointing at me in government and other official quarters.

Normal free access to such sources might become less easy, the informal off-the-record talks for guidance, the unsourced raw material columns of analysis and interpretation might become less forthcoming.
That was the situation when I met Chakravarti Rajagopalachari, a minister of the interim government.

He wondered what was behind my interview with Jinnah, particularly the question about the corridor. I told him the interview was but one of a series: the first had been with Gandhi, now this one with Jinnah. I hoped Nehru would be the subject of the third.

Rajagopalachari said he imagined I realised that as a result of that interview I might now find it rather difficult to go on working in my usual way. He had been discussing the interview -- and the corridor -- with the Mahatma. Gandhi told him he had met me and had formed the impression that I was "an honest young man".
So Rajagopalachari wanted to meet me and now, having done so, he would like to do what he could to correct the situation and enable me to carry on working as normally as possible.

Very deliberately and looking directly first at me and then at Ramachandran, who had not opened his mouth and now sat staring at the floor, Rajagopalachari said :"Are you sure, Mr Campbell, that you thought of that question? Or did someone else think of it and suggest it to you?"
Although he was a very dark Indian, I thought Ramachandran blushed when Rajagopalachari said that. Fortunately the minister did not pursue the question or seek an answer.

Instead he started to draft a short statement about journalism being a strange craft or profession in that young men practising it may not always be politically mature and could sometimes find themselves projected into headlines which were not of their seeking.

And so on. To any hard-nosed newshound it was pure waffle, guff, gobbledygook. It did not mention the Jinnah interview, much less the corridor or the fact that there was no ulterior motive behind either. But most newspapers published it and Indians, certainly those in government, politics and the media, knew it came from Rajagopalachari and knew the meaning of his message.
